prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and policy rules, which underpin the modern microfounded analysis of monetary policy

statement.case_for: My substantive configuration is unchanged: B012 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. My confidence in it is lower than in round 1, and it is lower for attribution reasons than for scientific ones. The case rests on three separable, identifiable contributions to one mature framework. Taylor's staggered contracts (late 1970s) were an early dynamic model of nominal rigidity. Calvo's time-dependent pricing (1983) gave the tractable building block of the New Keynesian Phillips curve. Woodford's microfounded framework turned these pieces into a normative and quantitative theory of monetary policy. The work is 25 to 45 years old and has been through the 2008 crisis and the 2021-23 inflation. In those episodes the framework was extended and modified, and it remains the common language of central-bank analysis. The Committee has not recognised this strand directly. I weigh breadth and durability of influence together with the clarity of the credit. I do not weigh how many colleagues rank it first. The round-1 exchange sharpened two points. First, Taylor's claim rests mainly on the contracts model, with the rule as the policy-facing part. Second, the question the chair posed is the right one. If the discovery is defined as the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms and their policy synthesis, the trio is defensible. If it is defined as the usable estimated policy framework, the Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler strand weighs more and a different cut would be needed. I read the discovery as the former. I accept that this is a judgement call on which reasonable members differ.
statement.case_against: Credit is diffuse. Eight names are credited on the ballot entry, and any three-person cut leaves out contributors who made the framework operational. B007 (Kiyotaki and Moore) and B026 (Melitz and Helpman) each have cleaner two-name attribution, and that is a real argument against my first choice. Calvo's time-dependent pricing is an assumption that micro price evidence qualifies, and the same issue applies to Taylor's contracts. The Taylor rule is closer to a robust regularity than to a deep theorem. The framework's record after 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation is contested, and the field is moving toward heterogeneous-agent models. No configuration has anything near six explicit supporters in round 1. I should not treat my own position as more than one of several plausible ones. I have not independently verified citation or priority details, and my assessment rests on the supplied evidence and my own reading of the literature.

responses.point: Friberg keeps Calvo in the trio as the originator of the New Keynesian Phillips curve mechanism, but he flags that micro evidence on state-dependent price adjustment challenges Calvo's time-dependence assumption.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and I know the micro-pricing literature from our joint work on menu costs. My view is that the evidence concerns refinement and not origination. Menu-cost and state-dependent models are also models of nominal rigidity, and they were built in dialogue with the time-dependent benchmark. The Calvo mechanism remains the tractable device through which most policy analysis is done. The critique applies equally to Taylor's time-dependent contracts, so it cannot decide between names. It does bear on the citation. I now prefer wording about nominal rigidities and the microfounded policy framework, and I would not credit Calvo's pricing assumption as the settled description of how firms adjust prices. If the Committee found the state-dependence evidence decisive against time-dependent pricing as a foundation, that would weaken B012 as a whole, not just one name.

responses.point: Andersson moved from Taylor, Woodford and Gali to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and says Gali is the natural substitute for Taylor if the Committee finds the rule unpersuasive.
responses.response: We now name the same trio, and I agree with his reasoning that Calvo is the more separable originator. I also agree with the substitution test, and I answer the chair's question directly. I would keep Taylor because the staggered-contracts model is a distinct early formalisation of nominal rigidity, separate from the rule. I would move to Gali only if the Committee decided that the discovery is the empirically evaluated New Keynesian model and not the origination of its mechanisms. Gali's work is arguably the best bridge between theory and data in this field. I would not oppose a Woodford-Gali-Calvo or Woodford-Gali-Taylor trio on scientific grounds, but I would then want the citation to say plainly that it honours the framework as used and not its origins.

responses.point: Krusell now prefers B007 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He says B012's diffuse credit and its post-2021 record weigh against it, while granting that B012's policy footprint is at least as large.
responses.response: I accept his attribution point as the strongest argument against my own configuration. Our disagreement is how much cleanliness of credit should offset breadth of influence. He rightly says that cleaner attribution does not make a discovery more important, and I try to apply that to B012 as well: three separable originators do not erase the omissions. On the merits I regard B007 as a clear, original mechanism that I rank second. I read the collateral-amplification mechanism as distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which weakens the overlap concern. I remain unpersuaded that it outweighs B012's reach into how policy is conducted. Krusell is my frequent co-author and IIES colleague, so I note that I am trying to weigh his argument on its content.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B026 with Melitz and Helpman. She values the combination of a conceptual advance with repeated testing against firm-level data across countries, and she treats selection and reallocation as distinct from the 2008 trade prize.
responses.response: I find her distinctness argument and her emphasis on repeated confirmation persuasive, and B026 is one of my two alternatives for those reasons. The unresolved issue is the credit boundary with Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, who are not on the ballot entry. A citation written about the heterogeneity-and-selection framework would partly answer it, as she suggests. My remaining difficulty is that Helpman's credit is also spread across other trade lines. Where we differ is how to compare an attribution problem that sits in the omissions of B026 with one in the choice among eight names in B012. I do not think the comparison is settled by the written record, and I would not claim it is.

responses.point: Boppart prefers Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He argues that their collateral mechanism is distinct from the 2022 prize, and that widening to Gertler would blur the discovery and re-open the Bernanke overlap.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow framing and with the argument that adding Gertler would blur the discovery. This is why I do not add Gertler to either B007 or B012. His credit competes between the two ballot entries, and I do not want it counted twice. Boppart is a co-author and IIES colleague, and I treat his argument as a case to be weighed on its content. I would support B007 as a serious prize on a clear mechanism. I rank it second because I weigh the breadth of the New Keynesian framework more heavily and judge the evidence for the collateral channel to be less clean.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee defines the B012 discovery as the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) or as the usable estimated policy framework, which would shift weight to Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler.
How much the micro evidence on state-dependent price adjustment and the 2021-23 inflation should reduce confidence in time-dependent pricing as a foundation, as opposed to prompting refinement.
Whether the Committee should prefer clean two-name attribution (B007 or B026) to a more influential but diffusely credited field, and how far my weighting of breadth is itself a judgement call.
Whether Kiyotaki-Moore is distinct enough from the 2022 prize, and whether the Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum omissions make a Melitz-Helpman pair premature.
Whether the one-person B026 part in a two-part B007 and B026 configuration (Strömberg) would be acceptable, which I have not resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No collaboration or institutional tie to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz or Helpman is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose co-authorship with committee members Krusell, Boppart and Friberg, and an IIES tie to Krusell and Boppart. My menu-costs research with Friberg and Ellingsen is close to the nominal-rigidities literature in B012, though it is not work by any credited candidate. My macroeconomics background is adjacent to B012 and B007. The 2018 prize background cites my own work, but that does not concern any shortlisted candidate. I am the chair and prefer B012, and the round-1 chair summary is a process record, not a ruling. These connections are disclosed, not adjudicated.
